design_detail: Cross-sectional online survey of US adults recruited on the Prolific panel, 1 to 9 October 2021, with quotas on sex, five age bands and five ethnic groups to mirror the US adult population (N = 2,822). Analyses use the 613 respondents who reported ever using any of seven classic psychedelics (ayahuasca, DMT, LSD, mescaline, peyote, San Pedro, psilocybin). All measures are retrospective self-report at one sitting: three items on challenging experiences (frequency, impairment of functioning, length of impairment) adapted from a meditation adverse-effects survey; a modified 11-item Meditation-Related Adverse Effects Scale (MRAES-MBP) for enduring effects attributed to psychedelics; a gladness item; the 26-item Challenging Experience Questionnaire (CEQ) for the respondent's most challenging lifetime experience; and checklists, for that experience, of set-and-setting factors the respondent associated with it, of what helped, of medications in use at the time, of thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others in the following days or weeks, and of help-seeking. Multiple linear regression (CEQ score) and logistic regression (any harm thought or attempt), with the 11 medication variables entered together in one model and the 10 set-and-setting variables together in another; no other covariates are stated. Appraised with ROBINS-E because the paper's analytic results, and the claims the before-and-during page will draw from it, are exposure-outcome associations; the prevalence figures are described with their sampling limits in the sample and key-findings fields.
can_establish: How often people in this quota-stratified opt-in online panel of US adults (October 2021) who had ever used a classic psychedelic reported challenging experiences, impairment, enduring symptoms they attributed to psychedelics, harm thoughts or attempts and help-seeking after their most challenging experience, and which retrospectively reported circumstances and medications went with higher CEQ scores and with harm thoughts or attempts among them.
cannot_establish: That any circumstance or medication caused a more difficult experience or harm (one retrospective survey in which the circumstances are respondents' own attributions recorded together with the outcome, with no demographic, psychiatric or use-history covariates); national prevalence in a probability-sample sense (an opt-in panel matched on three characteristics only); whether the actions respondents said helped did help; or anything about when the experiences happened, which substance or amount was taken, or how often people had used psychedelics.

sample.recruitment: Prolific Academic online panel, 1 to 9 October 2021; quota stratification on sex (2 groups), age (18-27, 28-37, 38-47, 48-57, 58+) and ethnicity (White, Mixed, Asian, Black, Other) to reflect the US adult population. Recruitment materials did not mention psychedelics (materials in the supplement). Payment of 2.20 US dollars; approval by the University of Wisconsin-Madison institutional review board (Materials and Methods › Participants and Procedure, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or over and currently resident in the US. No exclusion criteria, attention checks or data-quality exclusions are reported, and the number who started but did not finish is not given.
sample.demographics: Not reported in the article; key demographics of the 613 are in Supplemental Table 1 (a PDF supplement, not read). The article gives no age, sex, education, psychiatric history or number of lifetime psychedelic uses for the analysed group.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey). Non-completion, exclusions and item non-response are not reported; every table states 613 observations.
sample.selection_effects: An opt-in commercial panel with demographic quotas, not a probability sample; the authors note it may not be representative on other characteristics such as socioeconomic status (Discussion, 4th paragraph), yet the abstract calls it nationally representative. Lifetime use in the sample was 21.7% (613 of 2,822, editors' calculation). The paper does not compare this with a national survey, but it planned the sample from a published US prevalence estimate (its reference 17, by the same first author), expecting about 395 people with lifetime use among about 2,800 respondents, about 14.1% (editors' calculation); the panel gave about one and a half times that, which suggests that the opt-in panel over-represents people who have used psychedelics, or that use had risen (Materials and Methods › Participants and Procedure, 1st paragraph). People who died, are institutionalized or are not online panel members cannot appear. The 362 respondents who said they had never had a challenging experience still answered the CEQ and every most-challenging-experience checklist, so Table 2 and the regressions pool people with and without challenging experiences.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported checklist of lifetime use of seven classic psychedelics. For the most challenging experience: a multiple-choice list of set-and-setting factors the respondent judged to be associated with it (modified from Carbonaro et al., 2016; options in the supplement) and a checklist of 11 medication categories in use at the time. All recalled at one sitting with no biological verification; the date of, and time since, the experience were not asked or not reported (Materials and Methods › Measures › Most challenging, difficult, or distressing experience, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured: no amount, number of lifetime uses, route or date, and no record of which substance was taken on the most challenging occasion (respondents only named which psychedelics they associated with challenging experiences). 'Dose was too large' is a factor the respondent chose, not a measured dose.
exposure.polysubstance: 'Combining with other drug' was one of the factors respondents could attribute their experience to (4.4%). Use of alcohol, cannabis or other drugs was not measured as a covariate. Smoking cannabis (18.4%), drinking alcohol (8.8%) and taking another drug (3.6%) appear among the actions respondents reported as helpful during the experience (Table 2).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (retrospective survey of past experiences).

comparison.controls: Within the 613 people with lifetime use, respondents who did not tick a given factor or medication. The prevalence figures have no comparison group: the enduring-symptom items were not asked about periods without psychedelics, and no one without psychedelic use answered them.
comparison.matching: None. Each regression is mutually adjusted only within its block (medications entered together; set-and-setting factors entered together, Table 3 and Table 4 notes); no demographic, psychiatric, personality or use-history covariate is described, although the abstract and discussion call the models covariate-adjusted.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Psychiatric history (including the conditions for which lithium and other mood stabilizers are prescribed), personality traits that the authors cite as predictors of challenging experiences (neuroticism, Barrett et al., 2017), age at the experience, substance and amount, number of previous experiences, other drug use and socioeconomic position: none measured or used.

outcomes.instruments: CEQ (Barrett et al., 2016): 26 items rated 0 (none) to 5 (extreme) for the self-selected most challenging lifetime experience, Cronbach's alpha .97; how the total was scored is not stated. Frequency of challenging experiences (5 options), impaired ability to function (5 options) and length of impairment (6 options), adapted from items used by Goldberg et al. (2021) for meditation. Modified 11-item MRAES-MBP: enduring effects 'as a result of classic psychedelics' rated on a 5-point duration scale (never to more than 1 year), asked of everyone with lifetime use. Gladness item rated 1 to 6. Thoughts or attempts to hurt oneself or others in the days or weeks after the most challenging experience (4 items); sought medical, psychiatric or psychological assistance (yes or no); a checklist of helpful actions derived from Carbonaro et al. (2016).
outcomes.validity_norms: The CEQ was developed for psilocybin mushroom experiences; the frequency, impairment and duration items and the MRAES-MBP come from meditation research, and no validation for psychedelic experiences is reported. No norms and no comparison group.
outcomes.operationalization: A challenging experience is any answer other than 'Never' on the single frequency item. Degree of difficulty is the CEQ score for the respondent's most challenging experience, completed also by respondents who said they had never had one. 'Overall risk of harm' is any of the four harm thoughts or attempts in the following days or weeks. Each measure was rated once, retrospectively, by the respondent, at an unknown interval after the experience.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 42 counts the coefficient tests in Tables 3 and 4 (21 predictors against 2 outcomes; 2 could not be estimated in Table 4); descriptive prevalences are not counted. Editors' calculation: at a Bonferroni threshold of .00125 for 40 estimable tests, the lithium (p = .041 and .016), other mood stabilizer (.018, .015), no preparation (.010), disagreeable physical environment (.029), no psychological support for harm (.011) and major life event for harm (.022) results would not remain; only results printed as p < .001 might.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: respondents rated both the circumstances and the outcome themselves, knowing both.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 3 (CEQ, standardized beta, n = 613): no psychological support .25 (p < .001), dose too large .24 (p < .001), negative mindset .14 (p < .001), major life event before the experience .13 (p < .001), no preparation .09 (p = .010), disagreeable physical environment .09 (p = .029), disagreeable social environment .04 (p = .263), disagreeable music .05 (p = .192), combining with other drug -.06 (p = .099); lithium .11 (p = .041), other mood stabilizers .10 (p = .018), MAOIs .09 (p = .068), SSRIs .03 (p = .431). No intervals, unstandardized coefficients, R-squared or CEQ distribution. Table 4 (any harm thought or attempt, 41 events, adjusted odds ratios with 95% CI): negative mindset 4.56 (2.10 to 9.94), no psychological support 2.85 (1.27 to 6.42), major life event 2.93 (1.17 to 7.35), no preparation 1.17 (0.56 to 2.45), dose too large 1.60 (0.66 to 3.88), disagreeable physical environment 0.88 (0.33 to 2.35), disagreeable social environment 0.33 (0.11 to 1.01, p = .051), disagreeable music 2.67 (0.87 to 8.21); lithium 22.34 (1.78 to 279.65; 8 people exposed), other mood stabilizers 5.84 (1.40 to 24.34; 16 exposed), SSRIs 2.11 (0.61 to 7.37); St John's wort and haloperidol dropped. The printed p values agree with the intervals (editors' check on the log scale). Prevalences are printed without intervals; editors' 95% Wilson intervals: impairment longer than one day 55/613, 9.0% (7.0 to 11.5); any harm thought or attempt 6.7% (5.0 to 8.9); sought assistance 2.6% (1.6 to 4.2); severe impairment 4.6% (3.2 to 6.5).
analysis.covariates: None beyond mutual adjustment within each block of predictors; unadjusted estimates are in Supplemental Tables 2 and 3 (not read).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or preregistration is mentioned; the introduction describes the aims as exploratory. The data-availability sentence of the author manuscript still carries the journal-submission placeholder instead of a location for the data and Stata syntax.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports that 59.1% never had a challenging experience but not that 57.1% reported at least one enduring symptom they attributed to psychedelics, or that 6.7% reported harm thoughts or attempts. Unadjusted analyses and the sample's demographics are only in the supplement. The CEQ's scoring and distribution are not reported. The discussion does not mention that smoking cannabis and drinking alcohol were among the actions respondents reported as helpful, or the borderline inverse association of a disagreeable social environment with harm.
analysis.power: A priori: 395 people with lifetime use would give 80% power to detect a small R-squared increase at alpha .05 in linear regression (G*Power); about 2,800 respondents were sought to reach that number, from a published prevalence estimate (reference 17), and 613 were obtained (Materials and Methods › Participants and Procedure, 1st paragraph). Not addressed for the logistic models: 41 events for 9 and 10 predictors (about 4 events per predictor), with 8 people exposed to lithium, which yields an interval of 1.78 to 279.65.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In an opt-in panel matched to the US on sex, age and ethnicity, 59.1% of 613 people with lifetime classic psychedelic use said they had never had a challenging experience, 4.6% reported severe impairment of functioning, 9.0% (printed 8.9%) impairment lasting more than a day, 57.1% at least one symptom lasting at least a few days that they attributed to psychedelics, 6.7% thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others in the following days or weeks, and 2.6% help-seeking. Among the same respondents, attributing their most challenging experience to no psychological support, a dose they judged too large, a negative mindset, a major life event, no preparation or a disagreeable physical environment went with higher retrospective CEQ scores, and negative mindset, no psychological support and a major life event with higher odds of harm thoughts or attempts; lithium (8 people) and other mood stabilizers (16 people) were associated with both outcomes, with very wide intervals.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract describes the data as nationally representative of the US adult population and the models as "covariate-adjusted regression models" (Abstract), whereas the sample is an opt-in panel matched on three characteristics and the models adjust each predictor only for the others in its block. The discussion says the findings strengthen support for safety guidelines and judges it prudent for clinical trials and for legalization initiatives to follow current guidelines strictly until more is known (Discussion, 3rd paragraph), and proposes calming exercises such as mindfulness as preparation because 'trying to calm the mind' was the action most often reported as helpful (Discussion, 2nd paragraph), which is a self-report of helpfulness, not a test. The lithium interpretation draws on seizure reports, an outcome this survey did not measure, and does not consider that people taking lithium or mood stabilizers may differ in psychiatric history. Against this, the abstract uses associational language throughout, and the limitations paragraph states that no causal inference is possible, that representativeness covers only sex, age and ethnicity, and that self-report is open to bias (Discussion, 4th paragraph).

timeline.event: Carbonaro et al. survey of challenging experiences with psilocybin mushrooms (self-selected respondents), the source of this study's set-and-setting and helpful-action lists; the authors describe their own associations as consistent with it (as cited).
Barrett et al. develop the Challenging Experience Questionnaire used here (as cited).
Haijen et al. prospective study of predictors of responses to psychedelics, cited here for states and traits that predict challenging experiences
Nayak et al. analysis of online experience reports linking lithium co-use with seizures, cited for the lithium interpretation (as cited; seizures were not measured in this survey).
Simonsson et al. population-based survey of psychedelic-related seizures from an overlapping author group, also cited for the lithium interpretation (as cited).

This survey: prevalence of challenging experiences among people with lifetime use in a quota-stratified US panel, and cross-sectional associations with self-attributed set-and-setting factors and medication co-use.
Wood, McAlpine and Kamboj mixed-methods study of strategies for resolving challenging experiences, which cites this survey

replication.where_it_stands: No direct replication. The set-and-setting pattern agrees with earlier self-selected surveys as the authors say, but all such evidence is retrospective and self-attributed; whether preparation, support or mindset measured before use predicts the difficulty of an experience needs prospective designs such as Haijen et al. (2018). The lithium and mood-stabilizer associations rest on 8 and 16 people and are confounded by indication; they are a signal for pharmacovigilance, not an estimate.

funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the PMC author manuscript; the publisher's version (ScienceDirect) was not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Karolinska Institute, the University of Oxford, the University of Alabama at Birmingham, Monash University and the University of Wisconsin-Madison. Two of the studies cited in support of the findings (Simonsson et al., 2021 and 2022) and the meditation items adapted here (Goldberg et al., 2021) are the authors' own work. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people planning to use a classic psychedelic outside a laboratory, measuring mindset, preparation, recent life events, intended setting and support, medications and psychiatric history before use, and rating the experience with the CEQ within days, with analyses adjusted for substance, amount, personality and psychiatric history; for lithium and mood stabilizers, systematic pharmacovigilance or case-series data that record the indication and the acute effects.

domains.note: No control for confounding beyond mutual adjustment of exposures within each block. The lithium and mood-stabilizer associations are open to confounding by the conditions these drugs treat; the set-and-setting associations by personality, psychiatric history, substance and amount. None was measured.

Exposures are respondents' own attributions of their most challenging experience to listed factors, recalled at an unknown interval and reported together with the outcome; 'dose was too large' is a judgment, not a dose; medication use at the time is recalled.
Opt-in panel; the respondent chooses which experience counts as the most challenging; people with and without any challenging experience are analysed together.

Actions taken during the experience (changing location, help from friends, cannabis, alcohol) and later help-seeking could change both the CEQ rating and harm thoughts; they were not considered in the models.
Non-completion, exclusions and item non-response are not reported; every analysis has 613 observations.

CEQ and harm items rated retrospectively by the same person who reported the exposures, for an experience of unknown date; the CEQ was also completed by respondents who said they had never had a challenging experience; the frequency and impairment items gave inconsistent counts (see reporting issues).
No preregistration; 42 coefficient tests without correction; unadjusted results relegated to the supplement; no R-squared or CEQ distribution.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence of what predicts a difficult experience, the associations are at very high risk of bias: the predictors are respondents' retrospective attributions recorded with the outcome, nothing was measured before use, and no confounder was adjusted for. The prevalence figures are more useful but must carry their labels: an opt-in panel matched on sex, age and ethnicity only, unvalidated items borrowed from meditation research that gave inconsistent counts, and no comparison group for the enduring symptoms. Cite the paper for the proportions in this sample (for example 59.1% never had a challenging experience; 2.6% sought help) and, as hypothesis-generating, for the pattern that people who blame a negative mindset, lack of support or a recent life event report harder experiences. Do not cite it for any factor causing or preventing difficult experiences, for the effectiveness of what respondents said helped, or for a risk estimate for lithium or mood stabilizers.

key_findings.finding: Of 2,822 US adults recruited on Prolific with quotas on sex, age and ethnicity, 613 (21.7%, editors' calculation) reported ever using a classic psychedelic; all analyses are in these 613.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Materials and Methods › Participants and Procedure, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Frequency of challenging, difficult or distressing experiences with classic psychedelics: never 59.1% (362), rarely 23.3% (143), occasionally 13.1% (80), regularly 3.6% (22), frequently 1.0% (6).
key_findings.locator: Results › Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experiences, 1st paragraph; Table 1, frequency rows

key_findings.finding: Impaired ability to function: severely 4.6% (28), moderately 8.2% (50), somewhat 16.0% (98), not at all 32.6% (200), no difficulties 38.7% (237). Length of impairment: 1 day or less 33.8% (207), a few days to 1 week 4.4% (27), over 1 week to 1 month 1.1% (7), over 1 month to 1 year 2.3% (14), over 1 year 1.1% (7); longer than one day 55 people, printed as 8.9% (9.0% by editors' calculation, 95% Wilson interval 7.0 to 11.5).
key_findings.locator: Results › Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experiences, 1st paragraph; Table 1, impairment and length rows
key_findings.note: The two impairment items do not agree: 176 people reported some impairment of functioning but 262 gave an impairment length (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: 57.1% (350) reported at least one of the modified MRAES-MBP symptoms lasting at least a few days that they attributed to classic psychedelics: feeling anxious 36.1% (221), difficulty sleeping 27.9% (171), difficulty thinking or making decisions 24.0% (147), feeling disconnected from everything 23.7% (145), feeling cut off from other people 20.1% (123). Asked of all 613, including those reporting no challenging experience; no comparison with periods or people without psychedelic use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experiences, 1st paragraph; Table 1, symptom rows; Materials and Methods › Measures › Challenging, difficult, or distressing experiences, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: 78.6% agreed, from slightly to strongly, that they were glad to have used classic psychedelics (482 of 613, editors' sum: slightly agree 23.2%, agree 28.2%, strongly agree 27.2%); 21.4% disagreed to some degree, 5.9% strongly.

Challenging experiences were most often associated with LSD (24.0% of the 613; 31.5% of those who had used LSD), then tryptamines (ayahuasca, DMT, psilocybin: 15.3%; 19.7%) and phenethylamines (mescaline, peyote, San Pedro: 4.1%; 14.7%). Number of occasions of use of each substance was not measured.
key_findings.locator: Results › Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experiences, 1st paragraph; Table 1; footnote 2

key_findings.finding: Factors respondents associated with their most challenging experience (multiple choice, n = 613): no preparation 29.7% (182), negative mindset 15.7% (96), no psychological support 15.5% (95), disagreeable social environment 15.0% (92), disagreeable physical environment 14.5% (89), dose was too large 13.2% (81), major life event before the experience 6.9% (41), disagreeable music 4.9% (30), combining with another drug 4.4% (27).
key_findings.locator: Results › Most Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experience, 1st paragraph; Table 2, set and setting rows

key_findings.finding: Actions respondents reported as helpful during their most challenging experience (multiple choice, n = 613, helpfulness self-rated and not tested): trying to calm the mind 41.9% (257), changing location 27.4% (168), asking a friend for help 20.2% (124), changing the social environment 20.2% (124), smoking cannabis 18.4% (113), changing the music 16.2% (99), changing the environment in another way 12.6% (77), drinking alcohol 8.8% (54), using the body to shift the experience 7.8% (48), taking another drug 3.6% (22).
key_findings.locator: Results › Most Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experience, 1st paragraph; Table 2, helpful interventions rows

key_findings.finding: In the days or weeks after the most challenging experience, 6.7% (41) reported thoughts or attempts to hurt themselves or others: thoughts of hurting oneself 4.6% (28), thoughts of hurting others 2.6% (16), attempts to harm oneself 1.5% (9), attempts to harm others 0.7% (4); 2.6% (16; 95% Wilson interval 1.6 to 4.2, editors' calculation) sought medical, psychiatric or psychological assistance.
key_findings.locator: Results › Most Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experience, 1st paragraph; Table 2, risk-of-harm and sought-assistance rows

key_findings.finding: 11.3% (69) reported using at least one listed medication at the time of their most challenging experience: SSRIs 5.2% (32), other mood stabilizers 2.6% (16), SNRIs 1.8% (11), other serotonergic medicines or supplements 1.8% (11), tricyclic antidepressants 1.5% (9), lithium 1.3% (8), other antipsychotics 1.1% (7), methadone or buprenorphine 1.1% (7), MAOIs 0.8% (5), haloperidol 0.8% (5), St John's wort 0.5% (3).

CEQ score for the most challenging experience (standardized beta, set-and-setting factors entered together, n = 613): no psychological support .25, dose too large .24, negative mindset .14, major life event .13 (all p < .001), no preparation .09 (p = .010), disagreeable physical environment .09 (p = .029); disagreeable social environment, disagreeable music and combining with another drug not associated (p = .263, .192, .099). Medications entered together: lithium .11 (p = .041), other mood stabilizers .10 (p = .018); no other medication associated.
key_findings.locator: Results › Most Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experience, 2nd paragraph; Table 3 and its note

key_findings.finding: Any harm thought or attempt afterwards (41 events, adjusted odds ratios, 95% CI): negative mindset 4.56 (2.10 to 9.94), no psychological support 2.85 (1.27 to 6.42), major life event 2.93 (1.17 to 7.35); no preparation 1.17 (0.56 to 2.45), dose too large 1.60 (0.66 to 3.88) and disagreeable physical environment 0.88 (0.33 to 2.35) not associated; disagreeable social environment 0.33 (0.11 to 1.01, p = .051). Lithium 22.34 (1.78 to 279.65; 8 exposed) and other mood stabilizers 5.84 (1.40 to 24.34; 16 exposed); St John's wort and haloperidol were dropped from the model.
key_findings.locator: Results › Most Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experience, 3rd paragraph; Table 4 and its note

key_findings.finding: Adjustment: in both Tables 3 and 4 the medication variables were entered together in one model and the set-and-setting variables together in another; no demographic or clinical covariate is described, and unadjusted results are in Supplemental Tables 2 and 3.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Measures › Statistical Analyses; Table 3 note; Table 4 note; Results › Most Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experience, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the associations cannot show causality because of the cross-sectional design, that Prolific allowed stratification on sex, age and ethnicity only, so the sample may not be representative on other characteristics such as socioeconomic status, and that self-report is open to bias.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives 'major life event prior to experience' as 6.9% with a count of 41; 41 of 613 is 6.7% (6.9% would be about 42 people). The same count, 41, is correctly printed as 6.7% for any harm thought or attempt in the same table.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2, set and setting rows ('Major life event prior to experience') and risk-of-harm rows
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the count or the percentage is wrong; quote the count (41) with 6.7%, or both with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: Impairment lasting longer than one day is given as 8.9% (abstract, results, discussion), the sum of the rounded row percentages (4.4 + 1.1 + 2.3 + 1.1); the counts in Table 1 give 55 of 613, 9.0%.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results › Challenging, Difficult, or Distressing Experiences, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Table 1, length of impairment rows
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor rounding; the precise figure is 9.0% (editors' calculation).

reporting_issues.issue: The three challenging-experience items give inconsistent counts: 362 said they had never had a challenging experience but only 237 chose 'not applicable, I have not had difficulties' on the impairment item; 176 reported some impairment of functioning (somewhat, moderately or severely), yet 262 reported an impairment length (207 of them 1 day or less).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1, frequency, impaired ability to function and length of impairment rows
reporting_issues.consequence: Respondents appear to have read the items differently (for example reporting the length of the experience rather than of impairment); the impairment prevalence depends on which item is used (28.7% or 42.7%, editors' calculation), and the headline 8.9% comes from the length item.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and discussion describe the regressions as covariate-adjusted, but the table notes state only that the medication variables and the set-and-setting variables were each entered simultaneously; no demographic, psychiatric or use-history covariate appears anywhere.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Materials and Methods › Measures › Statistical Analyses; Table 3 note; Table 4 note
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may assume the associations, notably those for lithium and mood stabilizers, were adjusted for confounders; they were adjusted only for the other predictors in the same block.

reporting_issues.issue: The CEQ's scoring (sum or mean) and its distribution (mean, SD, range) are not reported, and Table 3 gives only standardized coefficients without intervals or R-squared.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Materials and Methods › Measures › Most challenging, difficult, or distressing experience, 1st paragraph; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the associations cannot be expressed in CEQ points or judged for clinical meaning.

reporting_issues.issue: The author manuscript's data-availability sentence still carries the submission placeholder where the location of the data and Stata syntax should be.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Materials and Methods › Participants and Procedure, 2nd paragraph, last sentence
reporting_issues.consequence: The data and syntax cannot be located from this version; whether the published version supplies them was not checked (publisher's site not read).
